The Vendors Feature: Background & Vision

How it works, why it works that way, and an invitation to the people running similar efforts.

This page is for residents who take a deeper interest in how the vendor listings work — especially those who run, or help run, other vendor-recommendation efforts in Sun City. It explains what has been built, the reasoning behind the design choices, and where this could go with your help.

The problem being solved

Vendor recommendations are among the most requested and most valuable information residents share — and among the worst-preserved. In most places they live in scrolling feeds and group chats: a great recommendation posted in a group helps the people who happen to see it that week, then sinks. Six months later someone asks the same question and the answer is re-typed from memory, or lost. Search in these tools is weak, membership is closed, and nothing accumulates: the tenth recommendation for the same plumber carries no more weight than the first.

The most organized efforts go further — a dedicated volunteer collects submissions and periodically assembles them into a shared list posted back to the group. That work proves how much residents value a real directory, and it deserves credit. It also shows the limits of hand assembly: the result is a snapshot that ages between updates, it is only as browsable as a document in a group's files area, it reaches only that group's members, and the whole thing rests on one person's continuing labor.

The guide's vendor feature is an attempt to give those same community recommendations a durable, structured, searchable home — without losing what makes them trustworthy, which is that they come from neighbors, and without asking any one volunteer to assemble it by hand forever.

How it works today

The heart of it is a simple pipeline: recommend → review → publish.

  • Recommending. Any verified resident can submit a vendor they have personally used — name, category, contact details, and what the vendor did for them. Takes about a minute.
  • Review. Every submission is reviewed by an administrator before it appears: names and categories are normalized, and anything inappropriate is filtered. Nothing publishes automatically.
  • One listing per vendor. When several residents recommend the same vendor, the submissions merge into a single listing: recommendation counts add up (“Recommended by 3 residents”), contact details fill in from whichever submission had them, and comments combine. Repeat recommendations make a listing stronger, not noisier.
  • Browsing. The public vendors page shows every service category — plumbing to pet care to patios — with listings grouped, counted, and deep-linkable (e.g. /vendors/#plumbing). Featured placements at the top are sponsored listings drawn from the same resident-recommended pool, and labeled as such.
  • Wider search. Inside any category, a resident can also run a web search of nearby providers (Google-powered). Those results are clearly labeled as not resident-recommended — useful where our own list is still thin, and every web-found vendor who works out is a candidate for a real recommendation.
  • Ask the Guide. Signed-in residents can simply ask the community chat (“can anyone recommend a plumber?”) and get resident recommendations alongside nearby options, with the same labeling.
  • Problems. Residents can report a bad experience privately. Reports go only to the administrators — nothing negative is ever published — and repeated concerns about a vendor over a period may result in administrative removal from the list.

Design decisions, and why

Several choices here are deliberate, and worth explaining to anyone who has wrestled with the same trade-offs:

  • Curated, not open-posting. Open forums self-moderate through volume; a directory can't. Review-before- publish keeps quality high, keeps spam and self-promotion out, and means every listing is accountable to a named (but unpublished) recommender.
  • Positive-or-absent — no published negatives. Publishing complaints about named local businesses invites disputes and legal exposure that a resident-run effort should not carry, and one-sided accounts presented as fact don't serve residents either. Instead, concerns are collected privately, patterns are watched, and the consequence is quiet removal. On a curated list, absence is the signal.
  • Verified residents, private identities. Recommending and reporting require resident sign-in — so every input is accountable — but recommender and reporter names are never published or shared. Listings show only counts.
  • Structured records, not threads. A recommendation captured as data (category, contacts, count) can be browsed, searched, merged, counted, and cited by the chat assistant. A recommendation captured as a chat message can only be scrolled past.
  • The web search knows its place. The wider Google search is bounded to our service categories (which keeps its costs controlled and predictable) and its results are always labeled as not resident-recommended. It supplements the community's knowledge; it never impersonates it.
  • No platform lock-in. The entire vendor database lives in a spreadsheet an administrator can read, edit, and export. If this effort ever ends or changes hands, the community's accumulated recommendations are a file, not a hostage.

Where it stands

As of mid-2026 the list holds 50+ vendors across 30+ service categories, seeded from resident-shared lists and growing through the recommendation form. The vendors page, the categories, the recommendation and reporting forms, the web-search augmentation, and the chat integration described above are all live.

The vision — and an invitation

Sun City already has residents doing this work — notably the vendor-recommendation Facebook group and the TeamReach group. Those communities have something this system doesn't: active conversation, trust built over years, and a large accumulated body of recommendations. This system has what the feeds lack: permanence, structure, search, and a home that any resident can reach without joining anything.

Those are complementary strengths, not competing ones. The groups are where recommendations happen; this can be where they last. Some concrete forms collaboration could take, in increasing order of ambition:

  • Cross-linking. The groups point members at the vendors page as the durable reference; the guide points residents who want discussion toward the groups.
  • Importing the archive — where that's possible. Where an administrator already maintains an assembled list of their group's recommendations, that list could — with their blessing — be reviewed and folded into the structured directory, preserving years of community knowledge in one step. Where platform rules make exporting past posts impractical, the path is prospective instead: the group shares a link to the recommendation form and encourages members to submit there in addition to posting in the group — the conversation stays where it lives, and the recommendation also lands somewhere permanent.
  • Shared stewardship. Group administrators — some of whom already collect and assemble recommendations by hand — are exactly the right people to help review submissions, watch categories they know well, or shape policy. This system automates the assembly, publishing, merging, and counting; the human judgment stays, shared among more hands.
  • Consolidation, if and when it earns it. If this system proves itself the better home, groups could retire their parallel record-keeping in its favor — on their timeline, by their choice.

If you help run one of these efforts and any of this interests you — or you think parts of it are wrong — please reach out through the contact form. Skeptical feedback is as welcome as enthusiasm; you know failure modes of this work that I haven't hit yet.

The guide is an independent, resident-created project — not an official Community Association service. Vendor listings are a convenience, not an endorsement; residents should use their own judgment when hiring. See the about page for the full picture.
